system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You are a 60-year-old woman with liver cirrhosis (severe scarring of the liver). You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours.

You were admitted from the emergency unit on 09/18/2022 because you had low oxygen levels (85% room air desaturation), were confused (obtunded), had bluish skin (peripheral cyanosis), and a mottled skin pattern (livedo reticularis). You were immediately put on a breathing tube (orotracheal intubation) without any problems. You had been feeling breathless since that morning. Before admission, you were given 4 injections of furosemide (a water pill) but did not pass any urine.

When you were admitted, you were on a breathing tube, sedated (given medicines to make you sleep) with midazolam and fentanyl, and given rocuronium (a muscle relaxant). Your blood pressure was stable with norepinephrine (a medicine to raise BP).

During your hospital stay, doctors thought you had acute respiratory failure (sudden lung failure) due to coronavirus, fluid buildup in the lungs (congestion), or a severe infection (sepsis) in your lungs. You had a coronavirus infection in March, confirmed by an RTPCR test on 03/15.

You were started on ceftriaxone (an antibiotic to fight infection). A paracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from the abdomen) was done, and there were no signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (an infection of the abdominal fluid). On the same day, a thoracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from around the lungs) was done, removing 1000 ml of fluid, which was a transudate (a type of fluid buildup). Another paracentesis was done, removing 4000 ml of fluid, and you were given albumin (a protein) because of the large fluid removal.

On 09/19, an ultrasound (POCUS) showed lines and thickening around your lungs, which, along with your breathing failure and need for BP-raising medicines, strongly suggested a lung infection (sepsis of pulmonary focus) as the cause of your breathing problems. So, clarithromycin and clindamycin (more antibiotics) were added.

On 09/24, after blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) showed growth of Staphylococcus aureus (a type of bacteria), your antibiotics were changed from ceftriaxone and clarithromycin to levofloxacin and oxacillin, as advised by [organization]. On the same day, an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was requested to check for endocarditis (infection of the heart valves) because of the bacteria found in your blood.

On 09/27 morning, your antibiotics were changed again to meropenem and oxacillin because your CRP (a marker of inflammation) worsened, and you needed more BP-raising medicines.

You slowly improved with your breathing and were taken off the breathing tube (extubation) on 10/03. Supplemental oxygen was stopped on 10/13. Your infection (septic condition) resolved, and you completed your antibiotic course on 10/08.

You remained in the hospital because you needed 24-hour nursing care, treatment for pressure injuries (bedsores), oxygen therapy, and management of ascites (fluid in the abdomen) and pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs). You did not have social support to go home.

You have a history of liver cirrhosis, first diagnosed in 2019, with the cause still being investigated. You have had complications like ascites, shp (hepatopulmonary syndrome, a lung problem due to liver disease) with medium-sized varices (swollen veins), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, eh (hepatic encephalopathy, brain dysfunction due to liver disease), and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

You also have a history of diabetes (sugar) for 15 years, hypertension (high BP) for 10 years, and a non-toxic multinodular goiter (swelling in the thyroid gland) diagnosed in 2019. You have anxiety and depression, diagnosed 6 years ago, and spondyloarthrosis (arthritis of the spine) with low back pain. You have a painful lump in your right breast, which was biopsied in November 2019 and was likely a fibroadenoma (a non-cancerous lump).

You used to smoke one pack a day for a few months and drank 3-4 cans of beer on weekends but stopped 2 years ago. You deny using illicit drugs.

Before this hospitalization, you were taking several medications: Insulin NPH (for sugar), Glifage XR 500 mg (for sugar), Simvastatin 20 mg/day (for cholesterol), Losartan 50 mg (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (a water pill), Sertraline 50 mg (for depression), Gabapentin 300 mg/day (for nerve pain), Calcium and vitamin D, Amitriptyline 25 mg (for depression/nerve pain), Propranolol 10 mg (for BP and varices), Omeprazole 40 mg (for acidity), Furosemide 40 mg twice a day (a water pill), and Spironolactone 50 mg/d (a water pill).

On 02/09/2022, you had a consultation where your furosemide was increased to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone to 50 mg/d due to massive ascites (a lot of fluid in the abdomen), dyspnea (breathlessness), and weight gain. A paracentesis was done, draining 4.1 liters of fluid. Another paracentesis was done on 09/13, draining 1.4 liters.

During this admission, you had several thoracentesis procedures: on 09/19, 09/23 (drained 700 ml), 10/06 (drained 1000 ml), 10/10 (drained 1000 ml), and 10/15 (drained 1000 ml). The fluid was a transudate, and cultures were negative.

Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus on 09/19, Staphylococcus epidermidis on 09/24, and Staphylococcus capitis on 09/28. All were resistant to oxacillin. Urine, pleural fluid, ascitic fluid, and catheter tip cultures were negative.

A CT scan on 09/21 showed bilateral pulmonary opacities (shadows in both lungs) that could be fluid or inflammation, bilateral pleural effusion (fluid around both lungs) with atelectasis (collapsed lung areas) in the lower parts, and cardiomegaly (enlarged heart). An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction (heart's pumping strength) of 59%, a dilated left atrium (upper heart chamber), preserved ventricular systolic performance (normal squeezing of the main pumping chambers), normal heart wall movement, mild mitral and tricuspid valve insufficiency (mild leakage of heart valves), and mild left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (mild problem with heart relaxing).

Your plan for discharge includes adjusting your water pill doses, closely watching your kidney function, continuing relief paracentesis and thoracentesis as needed, gradually reducing oxygen therapy, assessing if the feeding tube (nasoenteric tube) can be removed if you eat well by mouth, and caring for your pressure injuries on your back and hips. You have a follow-up appointment at AGAF on 01/18. Your family has been informed about the seriousness of your condition and the possible outcomes, and a shared decision was made not to perform any new invasive procedures.
